newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: British mercenary appears in court in PNG.
newsitem.headline: British mercenary appears in court in PNG.

text.p: A retired British colonel who led a group of 70 African mercenaries into Papua New Guinea but was foiled by an army revolt pleaded not guilty on Monday to illegally possessing a pistol and ammunition.
Colonel Tim Spicer, whose career in the British army saw a spell as a top U.N. peacekeeper in Bosnia, defended the abortive mercenary operation which has left this South Pacific nation in turmoil.
"There is nothing wrong with the activities of Sandline," Spicer told reporters as he left a court in the Port Moresby suburb of Boroko.
Spicer is chief executive of Sandline International, the British company which had a $36 million contract with the PNG government to crush an ethnic uprising on copper-rich Bougainville island.
He was detained last week as the other mercenaries left the country and the court decided on Monday that he should face trial on April 8.
PNG's crisis, the worst in its 22 years of independence, began last week when army chief Jerry Singirok demanded that Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan quit over the plan to use Sandline mercenaries.
Singirok was promptly sacked but remains in effective control of the army and has continued to put pressure on the embattled Chan.
Chan's government confirmed on Monday that it had removed Colonel Alfred Aikung as acting defence force chief and replaced him with Colonel Jack Tuat, who is seen as a Singirok ally.
Aikung, an army outsider who started his military career in PNG's small navy, was chosen to replace Singirok last week, only to be confined to barracks by his troops.
Chan, prime minister since 1994, said on Sunday he would not be resigning, telling the nation in a televised address: "We must uphold the constitution of Papua New Guinea."

But pressure mounted on Chan to resign over the mercenary contract -- described as a "stupid mistake" by Sir Michael Somare, the "father of the nation" who was PNG's first prime minister after it won independence from Australia in 1975.
PNG's governor-general, Sir Wiwa Korowi, also entered the fray. Korowi called a meeting of "constitutional office holders" for Monday to advise Chan on "how to take the heat off" in the row.
PNG is a member of the British Commonwealth and Korowi, as Queen Elizabeth's representative in the nation, is official head of state.
In a statement reported by local media, Korowi was deeply critical of the Sandline contract.
"There is no government house seal on it, nor had it been signed by me. It is a flaw of this type that throws this country's credibility to the dogs," he said.
And he warned Chan and two close allies, Deputy Prime Minister Chris Haiveta and Defence Minister Mathias Ijape, that they were "not indispensable".
Sacked army chief Singirok has said Chan must quit by Tuesday when parliament sits again so that a caretaker government can be installed in the run-up to June elections.

Mercenary commander Spicer said he would be happy to testify before a government commission investigating the Sandline contract after the court refused a request for his passport to be returned to him.

The British soldier, dressed in blue jeans, blue shirt and sailing shoes without socks, looked tired but relaxed. He carried with him a sheaf of papers and two books -- one about the Vietnam war entitled "Victory at Any Cost" and a biography of Ian Fleming, the British author who created James Bond.
